newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. Rwanda tribunal arrests Belgian suspect.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda tribunal arrests Belgian suspect.

text.p: The U.N. Rwanda genocide tribunal on Wednesday seized a Belgian national after Kenyan police arrested dozens of illegal aliens in a major crackdown.

A statement by the tribunal said Georges Ruggiu, the first non-Rwandan seized by court, was arrested in the Kenyan capital Nairobi and transferred to the tribunal headquarters in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha.
Ruggiu worked as a presenter for Radio Mille Collines during the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
He is alleged to have made numerous broadcasts in French inciting violence against ethnic Tutsis, politically moderate Hutus and Belgian nationals.

"We again thank the government of Kenya for its cooperation with the tribunal in arrests and transferring suspects believed to have committed crimes of genocide in the territory of Rwanda in 1994," tribunal registrar Agwu Okali said in a statement.

Seven suspects including Rwanda's prime minister during the genocide Jean Kambanda were arrested in Nairobi last Friday, the fruit of what the tribunal calls a "new operational strategy." Two of the suspects were indicted.

Kenyan police rounded up 80 Rwandans in Nairobi a day later. The privately owned Nation newspaper reported that 70 more foreigners, including Rwandans, were arrested on Monday night but a police spokesman could not confirm this.
Assistant Police Commissioner Peter Kimanthi denied the roundup was linked to the Rwanda tribunal and said it was a normal sweep to pick up illegal aliens living in Kenya.
Authorities in the tiny Central African state on Wednesday welcomed last week's arrests and urged the tribunal to pursue those still at large.

A statement issued by the office of Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu heaped praise on the tribunal, the U.N. leadership and Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi for facilitating the arrests, the biggest swoop so far by the tribunal.
"The arrest of seven of the top Rwandan suspects is a possible signal that the court in Arusha is finally heading in the right direction," said the statement.

"The people of Rwanda, therefore, hope that the tribunal will maintain this momentum and diligently pursue and prosecute the genocide suspects, wherever they may be, as prescribed by its mandate," it said.

The statement signals a change of heart by Rwanda, which had criticised the tribunal for slowness and argued for the transfer of suspects to its own genocide trials where at least 32 people have so far been convicted and sentenced to death.
Life imprisonment is the tribunal's maximum penalty.
Rwanda's Vice-President Major-General Paul Kagame discussed with Moi the question of Hutus living in Nairobi during a visit last week which he said patched up relations between the two states.

Kenya's decision to grant safe haven to prominent Hutus connected to the government of Rwanda's late president Juvenal Habyarimana, whose political cronies masterminded the genocide, soured relations with the Rwanda government which came to power in 1994.
The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda was set up in November 1994 to bring to justice the leading architects of the 1994 genocide sparked by the assassination of Habyarimana.
Twenty-three suspects have been indicted and the tribunal held 19 in custody in Arusha before Wednesday's arrest. Three trials are in progress.
